analysis.one_liner: Requires stockbrokers to put customers' interests first, claws back executive bonuses tied to fraud, and ends guaranteed severance for fired underperforming executives.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in November 2009 with zero cosponsors, referred to the Senate Banking Committee, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have imposed a set of investor-protection rules on Wall Street and corporate boards. Stockbrokers giving advice to retail customers would have had to act solely in the customer's best interest, the same legal duty that applies to investment advisers, instead of being allowed to steer clients toward products that pay the broker more. Executives who knowingly broke securities laws would have had to pay back their bonuses and any profits from selling company stock during the violation, shareholders could sue to force that payback, and companies could no longer promise big severance packages to executives fired for poor performance. It would also have protected anonymous whistleblowers in investor lawsuits, restricted brokers from voting company shares in board elections without the shareholder's instruction, and required independent advisers for executive pay deals [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary retail investors, especially retirement savers who rely on broker advice without knowing their broker may earn more by recommending certain products. Shareholders generally, who gain new tools to claw back executive pay after fraud and to sue the helpers who assisted a fraud. Company employees, whose pension holdings would sit in companies whose executives face real financial consequences for cooking the books.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the SEC to require that all brokers and dealers giving investment advice to retail customers owe those customers a fiduciary duty — the duty to act solely in the customer's best interest, ignoring the broker's own financial interest [S2] [S3].

Anyone who knowingly violates the securities laws must reimburse the company for any bonus or incentive- and equity-based compensation received during the violation, plus any profits made from selling the company's stock during that period [S2] [S3].
If a CEO or CFO fails to return pay after an accounting restatement within 90 days, a shareholder may sue on behalf of the company to recover it [S2] [S3].
Companies would be barred from listing their stock on exchanges if they award severance ('golden parachute') payments to a senior executive terminated for poor performance [S2] [S3].

Allegations from a confidential source would be treated as supporting a strong inference of fraudulent intent in securities fraud lawsuits, with protection for the source's confidentiality, making it easier for investors to bring fraud cases [S2] [S3].

The bill restores liability for people who provide substantial assistance to a securities fraud with reckless disregard — so banks, lawyers, and others who knowingly help a fraud can be sued alongside the principal violator [S2] [S3].
Brokers would be prohibited from voting customers' shares in board-of-director elections without specific instructions from the actual owner of the shares [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Full-service brokerage firms, whose sales-based advice model would be constrained by the fiduciary standard; corporate executives, who would forfeit bonuses and stock profits when they knowingly violate securities laws and could no longer count on rich severance after being fired for poor performance; and the banks, auditors, and law firms that assist issuers, who would face new exposure to lawsuits as aiders and abettors of fraud.

drawbacks.text: Applying a strict fiduciary duty to every broker could raise the cost of advice or push firms to stop serving small accounts, since the duty is expensive to comply with across millions of low-balance customers — a tradeoff Congress itself wrestled with in the parallel fiduciary-standard debate [S2] [S3].

The 'reckless disregard' aiding-and-abetting standard and the easier pleading rules for confidential-source allegations would expand securities litigation beyond the actual fraudsters, increasing legal costs and settlement pressure on banks, auditors, and advisers who were negligent at worst but not the primary wrongdoers [S2] [S3].

The bill leaves the definition of 'poor performance' to the determination of the company's own board of directors, a standard boards could apply loosely, and it gives existing compensation contracts a carve-out ('due regard for contracts in existence'), limiting how much the golden-parachute ban would change in place [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections — a best-interest standard for broker advice and clawing back pay after knowing fraud — are real and directly serve the people whose savings are at stake, and the fraud-liability provisions restore tools Congress had narrowed in earlier years. The honest objections are on the edges: the fiduciary mandate could price some small investors out of advice, and the expanded liability rules would raise litigation costs for third parties beyond the true wrongdoers. On balance the bill's benefits to ordinary investors outweigh those costs, though a careful drafter could tune the litigation provisions.

outcome.mechanism: A single senator introduced it, the Senate Banking Committee took no action on it, and it expired when the two-year Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Senator Robert Menendez introduced the bill on November 20, 2009 [S1] [S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day; that referral was the only committee action the bill ever received [S5].
No other senator cosponsored the bill — the cosponsor count was zero [S4].
The full action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote at any point before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Full-service brokerage firms and corporate executives are better off because the bill died: they never faced the fiduciary duty, bonus clawbacks, litigation exposure, or the ban on severance for executives fired for poor performance. Retail investors gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor; no other senator signed on.

against.name: Sen. Christopher Dodd
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Chaired the Banking Committee through the 111th Congress and never brought the bill to a hearing, markup, or vote; the committee referred it to no further action.

against.name: Securities industry trade groups and brokerage firms
against.role: Wall Street brokerage and investment industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed investor-protection mandates such as a broker fiduciary standard during the 2009-2010 financial reform debate.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and the partisan shape is unknown beyond the fact that the bill's only sponsor was a Democrat and no other senator, from either party, cosponsored it.

industries.note: The bill would force brokers advising retail customers to act solely in the customer's interest, ending the current rule that lets brokers recommend higher-commission products they personally profit from. Retail savers would keep more of their returns; the firms would lose a lucrative conflict of interest.

Executives who knowingly violate securities laws would have to repay bonuses and stock-trading profits, shareholders could sue to enforce that, and companies could lose their listings if they pay severance to executives fired for poor performance. Executives' pay protections come directly out of shareholders' and employees' pockets.

The bill would require any adviser helping set executive pay to be independent of the company and its executives, to report only to the board's compensation committee, and to be barred from indemnification — cutting consultants who profit from cozy relationships with the executives they advise out of that business.

industries.industry: Banks, auditors, and law firms that assist issuers
industries.note: The bill would make anyone who substantially assists a securities fraud with reckless disregard liable in private lawsuits to the same extent as the main violator. That deters gatekeepers from enabling fraud, but it also increases litigation costs for third parties who were negligent rather than intentional wrongdoers.
